name: PT Distribusi Voucher Nusantara Tbk

frontmatter.title: DIVA: a shrinking distributor priced at the value of its assets, with the bond written off
frontmatter.summary: DIVA distributes airtime, vouchers and digital payment hardware, and revenue is shrinking as the mobile operators sell direct. The balance sheet, not the P&L, is the story: our bridge credits cash, the listed portfolio, the associates and the share investment at evidence, and carries the affiliate bond at zero. The base asset value is the price and on its own is inside HOLD; the ADD rests on the model's convexity to a symmetric margin shock at a near-zero margin.
thesis: Revenue is in structural decline — operator direct channels are taking the voucher and airtime volume DIVA used to intermediate, and the hardware lines added since 2024 do not replace it.

The operating franchise earns a sub-cost-of-capital return, but it is only part of the value. The balance sheet holds cash, a listed securities portfolio, an affiliate bond, associates and a share investment, each of which the bridge values on its own evidence.

The market applies a blanket doubt to the whole balance sheet. The individual assets differ. The listed portfolio is marked at a third-party price, the share investment is already net of a large allowance, and only the bond and the related-party receivables carry real collection doubt.

The bond is written to zero, which is what its own note supports — overdue since its original 2022 maturity, interest waived, unsecured and with no repayment schedule. We no longer put a recovery rate on it, so the target does not depend on a judgement we cannot source.
A large minority interest and an insider-controlled register sit between the group's assets and the equity, and the free float is thin enough that any institutional position is expensive to exit.

catalysts.event: FY2026 audited financial statements, with the first full-year test of the margin recovery
Q1 2027 interim report, the first read on whether the revenue decline is decelerating
Annual general meeting, including any resolution on the retained deficit and dividends

blocks.text: **Rating ADD, target Rp98, total return 12.1% against a share price of Rp87 — the return is computed on the unrounded target.** DIVA is a distributor, not a platform: it buys airtime, data vouchers, e-money and bill-payment products from the mobile operators and sells them through a network of small retailers, agents and its own vending machines, earning a spread of a few percent on a very large gross transaction value [S3][S4]. The spread is real but thin — gross margin is 4.6% and operating margin 0.4% — and the business is shrinking: net sales fell from 4,173.5 in FY2024A to 3,504.9 in FY2025A and to 2,874.0 on our FY2026E estimate, with the nine-month 2026 figure already 2,123 IDR bn against 2,607 IDR bn a year earlier [S3][S4].

Our target is built from the operating business plus every asset the company owns, not from the accounting book at face. A discounted cash flow of the consolidated operations, after netting the short-term bank loans, deducting the minority interest in full, adding the trading-securities portfolio at its September market, crediting the associates at carrying value and the investment in shares net of its allowance, values the equity at Rp87 per share — within a rounding of the Rp87 the shares trade at [S3][S4]. Rolling that value forward one year at the cost of equity and applying a liquidity discount to the probability-weighted scenarios gives Rp98. The market pays Rp87, which values the reported book at 0.2x — a discount that is justified only if the assets behind the book are worth materially less than their carrying value.

This is the correction that matters since the first draft: the affiliate bond is now carried at zero. The note gives the nominal, IDR68.0bn, the waiver of interest because the issuer was loss-making, a maturity that has already been extended twice, and — in the collateral note — no security [S4]. Nothing in the filings values the Qerja equity into which it converts or any settlement, so a recovery rate was a number we could not source, and the whole premium to the price rested on it. At zero, the base asset value is the price. That is a much weaker call than the first draft, and the rating has to be read exactly: the base case alone, rolled forward at the cost of equity and discounted for liquidity, lands inside HOLD. What lifts the target to ADD is the probability-weighted tree, and the only reason the weighted value exceeds the base is the model's convexity to a symmetric margin shock at a near-zero base operating margin — it is not a bond recovery and not a portfolio option, neither of which is in any scenario value.

The variant view now has to stand on the assets the filings do evidence. About half of the group's assets are claims on related parties or marks on shares of other listed companies in the same group: trade receivables from related parties are 176 IDR bn of 189 IDR bn of total trade receivables, due from related parties is 58.0 IDR bn, the bond of affiliate PT Qerja Manfaat Bangsa is carried at 68.0 IDR bn, and the trading-securities portfolio is 58.4 IDR bn [S4]. Of those, only the listed shares carry a third-party price. The bridge therefore does not take book at face: the bond is at zero, the investment in shares is taken net of the allowance already booked, and the associates at carrying value. What is left of the variant view is narrower than it was: the market applies a blanket doubt to the whole balance sheet, when the listed portfolio and the share investment already stand at evidence and the doubtful claims are the bond — which we now write off ourselves — and the receivables, which sit inside the operating value rather than in the bridge.

The bear case in the tree is the operating bear only: revenue growth five points lower and gross margin one point lower, which takes the value to Rp73, below the price. It does not contain a receivables write-off or a further mark-down of the listed portfolio; those are a separate, unmodelled downside below it, and their size is not small — a full write-off of the 176 IDR bn of related-party trade receivables and the 58.0 IDR bn due from related parties would, on the shares in issue, be close to twice the per-share asset value of our base case (Rp87). The bull case in the tree is likewise the operating recovery the shocks produce — the same two drivers five points and one point above base, giving Rp166. The receivables aging being vindicated by collection and any re-rating of the shares off the assets rather than off the P&L are the market's response to that recovery, not inputs to the number; a settlement or conversion of the bond would be worth up to its IDR68.0bn nominal on top of it and is deliberately not credited in any scenario.

What moves the value, in order of importance: the operating margin, because at 0.4% a point of gross margin moves the DCF from near zero to a large multiple of the base; the mark on the trading portfolio, which moved by an unrealised amount of -40.9 IDR bn in the first nine months of 2026 alone; and the collection of the related-party receivables inside working capital [S4]. The bond no longer moves the value, because it is carried at zero. The operating forecast matters less than the P&L implies: the division earned 11.5 of operating profit on 2,874.0 of sales in our base year, and the balance sheet and the tails carry the rest. The rating is a statement about the probability-weighted path, not that the margin outcome is safe, and the margin is what the whole call turns on: the base case alone is worth the price and on its own rates HOLD, so the ADD is carried by the mirror-image scenario values rather than by the operating forecast; the sensitivity grid below says exactly how unsafe the margin is.

PT Distribusi Voucher Nusantara Tbk (DIVA) is an Indonesian distributor of digital products. It began commercial operations in 2003 and is domiciled in Jakarta; its own description of the business is a distributor of digital products with payment and online-to-offline platform activities [S4]. The economic model is simple and low-margin. DIVA buys airtime, data packages, electricity tokens, e-money and bill-payment products wholesale from the mobile operators and utility providers, and sells them through a network of small retailers, agents and its own self-service vending machines, keeping a spread on the transaction [S3][S4]. It is a volume business: gross transaction value is many times revenue, and the spread is a few percent.

The company reports four operating segments under PSAK 108: Digital Products and Services; Digital Financial Services; Travel and Tourism; and Other Ecosystem Generated Revenue [S6]. The first is the core and dominates both revenue and gross profit: it sells the vouchers and top-ups through the retail and agent network. Digital Financial Services is the second leg and is built around non-cash payment infrastructure rather than a balance sheet: e-money card top-ups through self-service vending machines at KAI and Jabodetabek LRT stations, and app-based parking payments under the PARKOUR brand at sites including Arunika Eatery, Menara Mandiri and a regional hospital [S6]. Travel and Tourism runs through a travel subsidiary, and the residual segment collects smaller ecosystem fees.

The group is a collection of small subsidiaries rather than a single operating company. The filings list Pawoon, a software-as-a-service point-of-sale and supply-chain platform in which the parent holds a minority economic stake, together with BTI, BKK, CBN, MDD, SI and Aviana, each operating in distribution, software, travel or related services [S4]. That structure matters for the equity story: the parent's reported profit depends on the subsidiaries and on intra-group balances between them, and the non-controlling interest that sits on the consolidated balance sheet is material.

Competitively, DIVA is a challenger in a commoditised layer of the value chain. It does not own the network, the spectrum or the brands whose products it sells; the operators do, and they increasingly sell directly through their own apps and modern retail. DIVA's assets are its retailer relationships, its vending-machine footprint and the payment integrations it has built with transport operators and municipalities [S6]. Management's stated strategy is to defend the distribution position through efficiency, to deepen the partner and UMKM ecosystem, and to add adjacent digital services such as the electric-motorcycle sales and rental initiative that also serves its sustainability reporting [S6]. Nothing in the filings quantifies market share, which is itself informative: there is no disclosed share position to defend.

Control is concentrated. PT Inti Dot Com holds 21.9%, PT Asuransi Jiwa Kresna 31.8%, PT Soteria Wicaksana Investama 15.2% and Martin Suharlie 8.2%; the public line is 20.9% and treasury 2.0%, and those blocks plus the public and treasury lines account for the whole register [S6]. Raymond Loho is the President Director, not a disclosed beneficial owner: the annual report names him as Direktur Utama and discloses PT Inti Dot Com as the parent, and we found no beneficial-ownership statement naming him [S6]. The company is run as part of a group of listed and unlisted vehicles rather than as an independent franchise, which is the origin of the related-party balances discussed in the governance section.

There is no published statistic for the voucher and airtime distribution layer in Indonesia, and the company does not cite one; its industry review instead describes the wider digital economy and the stress in the small-business segment that buys most of its products [S6]. What can be said from the filings is directional. The addressable market is the retail distribution of prepaid telco credit and digital services, and that market is being re-intermediated: the same operators whose products DIVA sells are pushing customers into their own apps and modern retail, and the company's revenue has fallen from 3,853.4 in FY2023A to 3,504.9 in FY2025A, the brief FY2024A rebound notwithstanding, and the decline is accelerating in 2026 [S3][S6]. Distribution does not disappear, but it shrinks as a share of the value chain when the supplier owns the customer relationship.

The demand side is the Indonesian consumer and the micro-retailer. The company's own review of the industry notes that financing quality in the small and medium enterprise segment weakened through 2025, with rising non-performing loans and a contraction in small-business credit, and that this feeds through to transaction activity in the digital ecosystem [S6]. That is the correct frame for DIVA: its customers are the warungs, agents and small kiosks whose working capital is under pressure, and their ability to pre-fund voucher inventory depends on the flow of credit to them. A recovery in that segment would help volume; a further deterioration shows up first in DIVA's receivables rather than in its sales line.

Competition in this layer is close to perfect. The products are homogeneous — an airtime top-up is identical whoever sells it — so the spread compresses to whatever the operator leaves in the channel, and the operator can withdraw it by pricing its own channel more attractively. There is no switching cost for a retailer that can buy the same stock from another aggregator, and no meaningful capital barrier to entry beyond working capital. What DIVA has built instead is a set of integrations: the vending machines in railway and light-rail stations, the parking-payment application, and the partner networks around them [S6]. Those are real but narrow advantages, and they sit in the financial-services segment rather than in the core voucher business.

Regulation cuts both ways. Digital financial services in Indonesia require licences and are supervised as to payment-system conduct and consumer protection, which raises the cost of the segment but also makes the incumbent's licence and integrations harder to replicate [S6]. The distribution of airtime and vouchers is lightly regulated, and that is precisely the part of the business that is eroding.

Our five-forces reading is unfavourable on four of five axes [S3][S6]. Supplier power is high and rising, because the mobile operators control the product and the customer. Buyer power is high, because retailers can substitute suppliers at no cost. The threat of substitutes is high and is the actual cause of the revenue decline. Rivalry is high among aggregators chasing a shrinking spread. Only the threat of new entrants is moderate, and the barrier is working capital rather than technology. The consequence for valuation is that we do not pay for growth in this business: incremental revenue consumes working capital and earns a return below the cost of capital, which is why our DCF does not pay for growth and why the equity value of Rp87 per share leans on the assets the balance sheet already holds.

The structure of the Indonesian prepaid distribution industry follows the structure of the mobile market. When subscriber growth was the operators' priority, third-party distributors were the cheapest way to reach rural and micro-retail customers; as penetration saturated and operators consolidated, direct digital channels became cheaper than paying a distributor's spread. Distributors that survived did so by adding payment, bill-payment and financial services to the same retail footprint, which is the strategy DIVA describes. The pattern is common to emerging-market distribution businesses and usually ends with the distributor either consolidating into a larger platform or shrinking to a niche of cash-based, low-income customers whom digital channels serve poorly.

The financial history is a distribution business losing volume while carrying a balance sheet built for a larger one. The annual report's three-year summary starts at FY2023A, at 3,853.4 of revenue; it rose to 4,173.5 and fell to 3,504.9 in FY2025A [S6]. We forecast 2,874.0 in FY2026E, 2,644.1 in FY2027E and 2,538.3 in FY2028E as the decline decelerates to flat, with no share recovery assumed because nothing in the filings evidences one [S3][S4]. The nine-month 2026 comparison already shows the shape: 2,123 IDR bn of net sales against 2,607 IDR bn a year earlier; the -18.0% figure we carry is the full-year estimate, not an annualisation of the nine-month rate [S4].

Gross margin has improved even as revenue fell, from 3.8% in FY2024A to 4.6% in FY2025A and 5.4% in our FY2026E, because the mix has moved toward digital products and away from low-margin starter packs [S3][S4]. The improvement is genuine but small in absolute terms: gross profit was 159.8 on 3,504.9 of sales. Operating costs are the problem. The cost base is sticky rather than fixed in rupiah: total operating expenses were 110 IDR bn in the first nine months of 2026 against the prior-year comparative in the same note, so they rose slightly while revenue fell, and the ratio is what moves [S4]. The model carries 143.7 of operating cost in FY2026E and 137.1 in FY2028E, a ratio of 5.0% rising to 5.4%, and operating profit falls from 15.4 to 11.5, an operating margin of 0.4% [S4]. By FY2028E the division is close to breakeven operating profit. We model no cost programme because none is disclosed.

The reported bottom line is not an operating number. In FY2023A the group recorded a net loss of -1,277.7 attributable to owners on operating profit of 9.7, because other income and expense swung to a large negative; FY2024A repeated the pattern on a smaller scale, and FY2025A reversed it, with other income turning positive enough to produce 46.5 of attributable profit on 15.4 of operating profit [S3][S6]. In the first nine months of 2026 the group lost -34.2 IDR bn, of which -40.9 IDR bn was an unrealised mark on the trading-securities portfolio; strip that out and the operating business is close to breakeven [S4]. A reader should therefore not treat the historical earnings line as a measure of the franchise.

Cash conversion is better than the loss suggests, and that is the one genuinely positive financial fact. Net cash from operations was 44.3 IDR bn in FY2025A, against -237.5 of reported loss in FY2024A when operating cash flow was negative, and it remained positive at 5.0 IDR bn in the first nine months of 2026 despite the reported loss [S3][S4]. The reason is that the losses are non-cash marks and impairments rather than cash burn, and that working capital has not released: trade receivables were 189 IDR bn, of which 176 IDR bn was owed by related parties, and inventories were 137 IDR bn at the end of September 2026, both large relative to a shrinking revenue base [S4]. We hold operating working capital roughly flat in absolute terms in our forecast — the NWC ratio rises to 13.8% of revenue — rather than booking the mechanical cash release a constant-ratio model would produce.

The balance sheet is liquid but encumbered. At 30 September 2026 the group held 45.8 IDR bn of cash against 12.2 IDR bn of short-term bank loans, so net cash is positive; equity attributable to owners was 598 IDR bn and non-controlling interests were 72.1 IDR bn [S4]. Four lines in the data pack are wrong and we restate them from the filing: cash at end-2025 is 42.1 IDR bn, not the pack's figure; balance-sheet cash at the latest date is the filing's own line, not the pack's larger number; debt is the bank-loan line, not the pack's line that sweeps in trade payables and customer deposits; and the investments line omits the trading-securities portfolio, which the filing carries at 58.4 IDR bn [S4]. Those restatements are recorded in the model and are the difference between a company that looks over-indebted and one that is not.

Capital allocation is passive. Capex is minimal — 0.8 in FY2025A, 1.4 in our FY2026E — because a distributor does not need plant; the vending-machine estate is the main capital item [S3]. The nine-month 2026 cash-flow statement already shows property-and-equipment spend above the ratio we carry for the full year, so FY2026E capex is modestly understated; the value effect is immaterial and we hold the ratio rather than fit to a nine-month run-rate, while flagging the gap here for the reader [S4]. No dividend has been paid and none is modelled, because the parent carries a retained deficit that must be cleared first [S4]. The cash that is not spent accumulates, which is why net cash is a real part of the valuation — and why the trading-securities portfolio, not the operating business, is where incremental capital has gone.

On the earnings-quality screens, the accruals picture is obscured rather than alarming: the gap between net loss and operating cash flow is driven by non-cash marks, not by receivables being capitalised into income, and cash has been ahead of earnings in each of the last two periods [S3][S4]. The divergence flags are real, however. Trade receivables have not fallen with revenue, and the overwhelming majority is due from related parties (176 IDR bn of 189 IDR bn); inventories of 137 IDR bn are large against a declining cost of sales [S4]. We found no special-notation or monitoring-board disclosure in the filings we read, and the audit opinion on the FY2025 accounts is unqualified [S3][S6]. The related-party exposure is quantified in the governance section.

A discounted cash flow is the right primary method here because the operating business is a spread on transaction volume with almost no capital intensity — capex ran at a fraction of a percent of revenue in the last two years — so free cash flow is close to EBITDA less working capital and tax [S3]. Multiples are a poor primary: the operating margin of 0.4% makes EV/EBIT meaningless, and EBITDA is small enough that a one-turn change moves the value more than any operating judgement. The asset side is not a cross-check bolted on afterwards: the group's value sits largely in cash, listed securities, the affiliate bond, associates and a share investment, and each of those is an explicit bridge item with its own source and its own treatment — the bond at zero, the portfolio at a third-party price, the share investment net of its allowance. That is why the model carries one method at full weight. A separate book-based method would count the same balance sheet twice: the DCF carries the operating assets, and the bridge carries the non-operating ones — the trading-securities portfolio, the associates, the share investment net of its allowance, the bond at zero, net cash and the non-controlling interest in full — so a book multiple would value those same assets a second time. The bridge is not offered as a walk through the 598 IDR bn of book equity; its net contribution is a small fraction of it, because the book is dominated by the operating balance sheet the DCF already owns. We therefore withdrew the adjusted-book weight we previously stated rather than apply a haircut twice. The weights differ from the industry default for the same reason: an EV/sales multiple on a distributor whose operating margin is a fraction of a percent carries no information, and the flag is answered in the model's justifications.

The cost of capital is built from the house Indonesia inputs and is not company-specific in its risk-free rate or equity premium, and the build is stated in full so that a reader can reproduce it. The ten-year risk-free rate is 7.4%, from which we deduct the house default spread of 1.6%, and we add the relevered beta of 1.29 multiplied by the sum of the mature-market equity premium of 4.2% and the country risk premium of 2.5% — that is 7.4% less 1.6% plus 1.29 times the sum of 4.2% and 2.5%, which gives the cost of equity of 14.5%. The industry unlevered beta is 1.20, relevered at a 10.0% debt-to-equity ratio at a 22.0% tax rate. With pre-tax cost of debt of 9.4%, the same 22.0% tax rate and a 9.1% debt weight, the WACC is 13.8%, against terminal growth of 2.0% [S3][S4]. The beta is the industry default rather than a regression on DIVA's own history, which is defensible for a company whose share price has moved more on asset marks than on operating news. The WACC and the cost of equity of 14.5% sit above the method card's band for IDR names, and we state why rather than move the inputs: the gap comes from the house risk-free rate of 7.4% and the country premium of 2.5%, not from a company-specific add-on — we apply no premium above the build. We keep the build because the group is loss-making at the net line and earns a fraction of a percent on sales, so there is no case for discounting it at the band midpoint. The value is also not rate-sensitive in the way the headline suggests: the WACC axis of the grid below moves the DCF by a few percent across a full point, while the margin axis moves it from zero to a multiple of the base.

The DCF produces an enterprise value of 84.0 from ten explicit years of free cash flow, with the terminal value only 25.2% of the total — the forecast is doing most of the work, which is what we want in a business with no credible long-term growth. The bridge then adds what the operating DCF does not contain: the trading-securities portfolio at its 30 September market of 58.4 IDR bn, the associates at 13.2 IDR bn of equity-method carrying value and the investment in shares at 5.2 IDR bn net of the allowance already booked, against the short-term bank loans of 12.2 IDR bn and the non-controlling interest of 72.1 IDR bn deducted in full. That gives Rp87 per share, and the bond of IDR68.0bn nominal contributes nothing to it. Writing the bond off is the only judgement in the bridge, and it is the conservative reading of its own note: the securities are at a third-party price, the share investment is already net of a large allowance, the associates are at the value the equity method carries after their losses, and the bond is unsecured, overdue since 2022 and interest-free by waiver [S4]. A settlement or conversion is therefore an option on top of Rp87 rather than a component of it.

The target applies the house construction. The base value is rolled forward one year at the cost of equity to Rp100, the three scenarios are weighted by probability to Rp108, and a 10.0% discount is applied for the size of the position a fund could actually build, giving Rp98 [S3][S4]. The discount is the house schedule for a name whose three-month average daily traded value is 1,681,808,182.5 [S0], not a judgement about the assets. The free float, taken from the annual report register rather than the data pack, is the public line of 20.9% with 2.0% in treasury [S6]. Both the pre-discount and post-discount values sit above the share price, so the rating does not turn on the discount; but both sit close to it, which is why the call is ADD rather than BUY.

The cross-checks bracket the answer without changing it. At Rp87 the shares trade on 0.2x of book and 5.9x EV/EBITDA. The price-to-book is the number that attracts value buyers, and it is now reconcilable: of the 598 IDR bn of book equity, the assets that carry real collection doubt are the 176 IDR bn of related-party trade receivables, the 58.0 IDR bn due from related parties and the 68.0 IDR bn bond; the rest is cash, the listed portfolio at a third-party price, inventory, property and third-party receivables [S4]. The write-off sits on the bond inside the bridge rather than on the whole book, and the share investment is already net of its allowance, so the value is not book-times-a-blanket-haircut: it is the book with the doubtful bond taken to zero and the listed marks taken at their own price. The 5.9x EV/EBITDA pairs today's price with FY2026E year-end net cash; on the current balance sheet the multiple is higher, because net cash is smaller now than at the forecast year-end. And because normalised EBITDA is above the FY2026E trough, the multiple on normalised earnings falls rather than rises — the screen does not argue that the shares are expensive.

The peer set does not supply a usable multiple, but it does tell us what the market pays for the same problem. BUKA and GOTO, both rated BUY in this book, are trading below or near their own cash and securities, which is the same arithmetic as DIVA's cash plus listed portfolio plus bond against the market capitalisation. BELI and TFAS are rated REDUCE and SELL on the opposite case: growth bought with margin, and a distributor priced as a platform. EMTK is a conglomerate held at a discount to its listed stakes. DIVA sits on the cheap side of that group on the assets and the expensive side on the operating franchise, which is precisely what a single-method DCF with an explicit bridge is meant to express. We do not import a peer multiple because the revenue models are not comparable — a voucher distributor's sales line is a pass-through of third-party product.

The grid is the honest statement of the model's weakness. With an operating margin of 0.4%, a one-point move in gross margin takes the one-year value from close to zero to a large multiple of the base, and the revenue axis is not monotonic either. That is why we state the base case and the bridge separately: the margin path is a coin flip inside any plausible range, while the bridge is evidenced item by item and bounds the downside. A reader who disagrees with the bridge should discount the target heavily; a reader who takes the base margin as given should not.

Working capital is the second lever and it explains the inverted revenue axis. Every extra rupiah of revenue has to carry net working capital at 13.8% rising to 15.6%, so growth at a margin below the cost of capital destroys value rather than creating it; a model that held the ratio constant would book a one-off cash release and overstate the value. Both levers are visible in the grid, and neither is a reason to prefer a more cautious base case: the base margin is the level the company is actually earning, and the working-capital path holds the balance-sheet balances broadly flat rather than assuming a release. The burden of proof sits on anyone who wants to move either.

What does the price imply? Solving the DCF for the FY2027E revenue growth that reproduces today's price gives -8.0%, against our forecast of -8.0% [S3][S4]. The mapping is not monotonic — in this model extra revenue absorbs working capital and earns below the cost of capital — so the solve is not unique and the number is not a growth forecast. We therefore draw no inference from it about what the market is pricing. The gap between the price and our asset-inclusive value is the variant view stated above, not something the reverse solve can confirm or deny.

The dominant risk is not operating, it is the recoverability of the intra-group balances, which are about half of the 714 IDR bn of total assets. Trade receivables from related parties of 176 IDR bn sit alongside 58.0 IDR bn due from related parties, the bond of 68.0 IDR bn and 58.4 IDR bn of trading securities, almost all of it claims on companies in the same group [S4]. The filing's own evidence cuts both ways. Of the 189 IDR bn of net trade receivables, 185 IDR bn was not yet due at 30 September 2026 and only 3.6 IDR bn was more than three months past due, against an allowance of 4.5 IDR bn; the balances are unimpaired and the opinion is unqualified [S4]. The bear reading is that the aging measures contractual status, not credit quality: the obligors are the same group vehicles whose shares DIVA marks at a loss, and the largest related-party balances are working-capital loans to them. The bull reading is that the balances are current, the allowance is what management believes adequate, and no write-off has been taken. We do not add the receivables to the bridge because the operating DCF already carries them in working capital; if they are not collected, it is the operating value that suffers, and that is why the bear scenario is a revenue and margin path rather than a separate receivables line. That is a limitation of the tree we state rather than paper over: the modelled bear does not contain the write-off, so the true downside is larger than Rp73, not equal to it. We rate the collection risk medium likelihood and high impact: the bond is already at zero in the bridge, but a write-down of the receivables would remove part of the operating value and would take the shares below the price on any margin assumption.

The second risk is the continuation of the revenue decline, which we regard as near-certain in direction and material in size. Operator direct channels are the cause, and they take share with no action required from DIVA; the -18.0% full-year decline we forecast is our base case, not a stress [S4]. If the decline runs faster, the sticky cost base turns an operating margin of 0.4% into a loss quickly, because gross margin is only 5.4%.

Third, the mark-to-market on the trading portfolio is a live earnings risk rather than a hypothetical one: -40.9 IDR bn of unrealised loss was recognised in the first nine months of 2026 on a portfolio carried at 58.4 IDR bn [S4]. A further fall in the group's listed shares flows straight through the P&L and the equity line, and it is not hedged.

Fourth, liquidity and ownership. The annual report register shows the public line at 20.9% and treasury at 2.0%, with the four disclosed blocks making up the rest; the three-month average daily traded value is 1,681,808,182.5 [S0][S6]. A fund that builds a position cannot exit it quickly, which is why the target carries a 10.0% discount, and the concentration means minority holders have no practical influence over related-party terms.

Fifth, governance and regulatory risk. The company operates licensed payment services, so a supervisory action against the financial-services segment would remove the one part of the business with defensible integrations [S6]. Auditor change, a qualified opinion or going-concern language would be a material negative signal; the FY2025 opinion was unqualified, so the bar is current [S3].

Sixth, macro and consumer risk. DIVA's customers are micro-retailers whose working capital depends on small-business credit; the company's own industry review notes rising small-business non-performing loans and contracting credit, which feeds directly into voucher demand [S6]. This is a second-order driver against the balance-sheet risks but it sets the pace of the operating decline.

The scenarios mirror each other on the two operating drivers and differ on nothing else in the shocks: bear takes 30.0% probability with revenue growth five points lower and gross margin one point lower than base, bull takes 25.0% with the same amounts higher, and base keeps 45.0% [S3][S4]. Each scenario carries the bond at zero, exactly as the base does, so the three values are directly comparable and none of them contains a recovery: Rp73 in the bear case, Rp100 in the base and Rp166 in the bull, a probability-weighted Rp108 before the liquidity discount. The tree is ordered bear below base below bull, and the bear value is below the Rp87 price, which is the downside we are asking a buyer to accept. The bear is the operating bear only — the two drivers shifted down, with no receivables write-off and no further mark-down of the listed portfolio inside it. A full write-off of the 176 IDR bn of related-party trade receivables and the 58.0 IDR bn due from related parties would sit below the whole tree: on the shares in issue it is close to twice the per-share asset value of the base case (Rp87), and it is why a buyer is being asked to take the operating bear as the modelled floor, not as the worst case. The bridge already carries the balance-sheet stress: the bond at zero, the share investment net of its allowance and the associates at carrying value. We keep the write-off as a stated stress rather than a fourth probability-weighted scenario because it is a balance-sheet event, not a revenue path, and the interim review found no impairment trigger [S4]. An asymmetry in the operating shocks would need a source; there is none, so the shocks are symmetric.

Two asymmetries are real and are stated rather than modelled. The bond's IDR68.0bn nominal can convert into 10.6% of Qerja or be repaid, and no document values either, so full recovery would add up to that nominal to any of the three values above while failure adds nothing to any of them — that is an option we do not price, in the bull or anywhere else [S4]. The trading portfolio can also mark up as well as down, and the -40.9 IDR bn unrealised loss already booked in the first nine months of 2026 is the size of the move in one direction [S4]. Neither asymmetry is in any scenario value, so neither can be the reason the weighted tree sits above the base. No bond recovery and no portfolio mark-up is credited in the bear, the base or the bull. The reason the weighted value exceeds the base is convexity: with a base operating margin of 0.4%, the same one-point gross-margin shift is worth far more on the upside than it costs on the downside, and the model reproduces that — the bull value is about two-thirds above the base and the bear about a quarter below it, so a symmetric shock produces an asymmetric average. That is the entire source of the Rp108 weighted value against the Rp100 base. We state the consequence plainly rather than dress it up: the base case alone, rolled at the cost of equity and discounted, is inside HOLD, and the ADD rests on this convexity, not on the base operating forecast and not on the two options above. A reader who believes a symmetric margin shock should produce symmetric values should hold the shares at the base roll.

Signposts that would change our view: disclosure of a collection schedule or settlement of the related-party receivables; a recovery in the group's listed shares that reverses the unrealised losses; any new material related-party transaction priced away from arm's length; evidence that the financial-services integrations are winning third-party contracts rather than group business; and a cost programme that holds the SG&A line flat in absolute terms as revenue falls. Any one of the first two would move us toward the bull case; any of the last two would move us toward the bear.

Ownership is the central governance fact. PT Inti Dot Com holds 21.9%, PT Asuransi Jiwa Kresna 31.8%, PT Soteria Wicaksana Investama 15.2% and Martin Suharlie 8.2%; the public line is 20.9% and treasury 2.0%, and those four blocks plus the public and treasury lines account for the whole register [S6]. Raymond Loho is the President Director, named in the annual report as Direktur Utama; the disclosed parent is PT Inti Dot Com, and the report contains no beneficial-ownership statement naming him, so we do not describe him as the UBO [S6]. The free float is the public line, with the treasury shares not free. No shareholder agreement, pledge or voting arrangement over the controlling stake is disclosed in the sections we read; we record that as an absence of evidence, not evidence of absence, and it is a gap a buyer should price.

The board structure is conventional for an IDX listing, with a board of commissioners including independent members and a separate statement of their independence, and a board of directors; the company employs 78.0 people, consistent with a distribution business that owns little plant [S6]. The FY2025 consolidated accounts were audited by KAP Mirawati Sensi Idris with an unqualified opinion under Indonesian Financial Accounting Standards [S3][S6]. There has been no auditor change in the periods we reviewed.

Related-party dealings are the governance exposure, and they are large rather than incidental. 176 IDR bn of the 189 IDR bn of trade receivables are due from related parties, a further 58.0 IDR bn is due from related parties outside trade, 68.0 IDR bn is invested in an affiliate's bonds and 58.4 IDR bn is held in shares of group companies — principally the listed vehicles whose marks drive the P&L [S4]. These are the assets that support book value, and they are transacted with parties under common control. The audit opinion is clean, which tells us the balances are fairly presented, not that they will be collected.

The bond is the clearest single governance fact. The bond note shows a convertible with 68.0 IDR bn of nominal issued to PT Qerja Manfaat Bangsa, an affiliate, bearing no interest and originally maturing on 29 September 2022 [S4]. An addendum introduced a coupon from that date, a second extended maturity to 31 December 2026, and in December 2024 the company waived the interest altogether because the issuer was making operating losses; the instrument is convertible into shares equal to 10.6% of the issuer and is still carried at par with no impairment [S4]. The company discloses no repayment schedule and no collateral [S4]. A four-year-overdue, unsecured, non-interest-bearing related-party instrument at par is a claim whose value the filing never establishes, and we therefore carry it at zero in the bridge. That is not a view that the conversion right is worthless — 10.6% of a loss-making affiliate is not obviously worth nothing — but a decision that we will not put a hand-typed recovery into the target, and it is the conservative reading of the only document that speaks to it.

Dividend record is nil. The parent carries a retained deficit, so no distribution is possible until earnings clear it, and we model no dividend through the forecast [S4]. Capital allocation has instead gone into the securities portfolio and into minority stakes in group ventures, which is the opposite of returning cash.

ESG exposures are modest relative to the governance ones but not zero. The company reports environmental and social programmes including electrification of its fleet through electric-motorcycle sales and rental, battery-swap points at operating offices, and community programmes under its sustainability report [S6]. The material environmental question for a distributor is electronic waste from vending machines and payment hardware and the energy footprint of its estate, neither of which is quantified in a way that affects our valuation. Socially, its exposure is the micro-retail customer base, which is also its credit risk. Governance is where the discount belongs.

The dated catalysts are the reporting calendar, because there is no event in the filings that is scheduled to change the operating picture. The FY2026 audited statements, expected by the end of March 2027, are the first full-year test of whether the gross-margin improvement survives a full year of falling revenue and whether the related-party balances show any sign of collection [S4]. The Q1 2027 interim follows by the end of April and is the first read on the deceleration; the annual general meeting in the second quarter is where any resolution on the retained deficit or a capital action would appear [S3].

Between reports we monitor six things. First, the quarterly rate of revenue decline against our -18.0% for FY2026E, because the operating case is entirely about the pace of the fall. Second, gross margin against 5.4%, the one line that has improved. Third, the split of trade receivables between related and third parties — a rise in the related-party share is the clearest warning [S4]. Fourth, the mark on the trading-securities portfolio and the share prices of the group's listed vehicles, which flow through the P&L. Fifth, the SG&A line in absolute rupiah, since a flat cost base against falling revenue is what turns the operating margin negative. Sixth, any new related-party transaction, auditor change or change in the controlling shareholding, each of which would force a re-underwrite rather than an update.

The monitoring threshold that matters most is not in the P&L at all: it is any disclosure that values, settles or impairs the intra-group balances. Until that happens, the shares are a claim on assets whose worth is asserted by the group rather than tested by a third party, and our target reflects that. The company publishes its annual reports and investor presentations on its own investor-relations site, which is where we would expect such a disclosure to appear first [S2].

S0.title: Yahoo Finance statements, prices and profile for DIVA.JK

bear.narrative: The operating decline steepens: voucher and airtime volume falls faster as operators move distribution in-house, gross margin is one point lower than base as the device lines fail to hold price, and trading losses on the TFAS/MCAS/NFCX stakes continue. The Qerja bond is at zero here exactly as in the base and the bull, and this branch carries no receivables write-off: a full write-off of the related-party balances is a balance-sheet stress that sits below the published tree, stated in the report and not probability-weighted [S4].

bull.narrative: The decline halts as the EV-parts and O2O device businesses scale and gross margin is one point higher than base, which is the operating recovery this branch values. The receivables aging being vindicated by collection, and any re-rating of the shares off a deep discount to the assets the bridge credits, are the market's response to that recovery: neither is an input to this number and the shocks are the two operating drivers only. The Qerja bond is carried at zero here exactly as in the base and the bear, so any settlement or conversion of the nominal is upside on top of it, stated in the report and not credited in the tree [S4].

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: 9M2026 net sales fell 18.6% y/y to Rp2,122.8bn as telco airtime/voucher distribution keeps migrating to the operators' own digital channels; the hardware and EV-parts lines added in 2024 do not offset it. We model the decline decelerating to -8%, -4% and flat by FY2029E as the low base and the residual B2B/O2O device base stabilise, then +1% nominal. No recovery in voucher share is assumed because nothing in the filings shows one.

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: 9M2026 gross margin was 5.42% (Rp115.1bn on Rp2,122.8bn), up from 4.56% in FY2025A as the mix shifted to digital products and away from low-margin starter packs. We hold the achieved 5.4-5.5% rather than the three-year average, because the improvement is already in the last actual period and is what the company is currently earning.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: The cost base is sticky rather than fixed in rupiah: total operating expenses were Rp109.7bn in 9M2026 against Rp105.7bn in 9M2025 (F9) while revenue fell, so the ratio is 5.17% of sales versus 4.12% in FY2025A. Costs rose 3.8% year on year, not zero, so the model carries the dollar line near Rp137bn and lets the ratio rise to 5.4% as revenue falls; no cost programme is disclosed in the filings.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: Capex is minimal in a distribution model: Rp0.8bn in FY2025A on Rp3,504.9bn of sales and Rp1.8bn in FY2024A, i.e. under 0.05% of revenue in both years. We hold the last actual ratio for EDC/vending-machine maintenance; a shrinking estate does not need more. Known and accepted understatement: the 3Q2026 cash-flow statement shows Rp1.78bn already spent on property and equipment in the nine months to 30 September 2026 [S4], above the Rp1.44bn this ratio implies for FY2026E; the value effect is under Rp0.3bn, and the FY2027E-onward ratio is the maintenance rate of a smaller estate rather than the 2026 build.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: No dividend has been paid and the parent carries a retained deficit of Rp61.2bn at 30 Sep 2026, so no distribution is possible until that is cleared; we model zero payout throughout.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: Capped at the house long-run nominal GDP for Indonesia (4%); we use 2% because the distribution volume is in structural decline offset by price inflation, with no share gains assumed.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A (div(da, revenue))

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Working capital does not release as revenue falls: revenue dropped 18.6% in 9M2026 while cash fell to Rp45.8bn from Rp42.1bn at December 2025 and receivables, inventory and due-from-related balances all rose (trade receivables Rp189.1bn, inventory Rp136.9bn, due from related parties Rp58.0bn). We therefore hold operating working capital roughly flat in absolute terms by letting the ratio rise against a falling revenue base, rather than booking the mechanical cash release a constant-ratio model would produce.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A (div(tax, pbt))

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A (div(interest_expense, debt[-1]))

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A (div(interest_income, cash[-1]))

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A (div(minority, np))

challenges.challenge: The DCF bridge credits only net cash -33.67, minorities -72.11 and investments 58.37. It omits three non-operating assets on the 30 September 2026 consolidated balance sheet: the Rp68.0bn convertible bond to PT Qerja Manfaat Bangsa (S4 note 16, carried at fair value 68.0), Rp13.19bn investment in associates and Rp5.23bn FVOCI shares. At 1,399.99m shares the bond alone is Rp48.6/share against a Rp67 target and a Rp87 price. This is not a defensible zero: fund record book_haircut says a 45% haircut is applied to the same bond, i.e. a Rp37.4bn value, and the report never says the bridge gives it nothing.
challenges.answer: Added valuation.bridge: Qerja bond Rp68.0bn at 55% recovery, associates Rp13.19bn and share investment Rp5.23bn at carrying value, all sourced to S4 note 16 and the 30 Sep 2026 balance sheet; target moves from Rp67 to Rp125 (BUY).

challenges.challenge: Section 4 says applying a haircut to the related-party items is what separates the Rp67 from a book-based value, and section 5 says a full impairment of those balances is covered by the asset haircut described in the valuation section. No such haircut exists in the valuation: fund record carries book_haircut 0.45 and valuation.weights with adjusted_book at 0.5, but fund record methods contains dcf_fcff only at weight 1.0, dropped_methods is empty, book_haircut is not an engine line, and qc returns weights.changed as justified false. The number is a pure operating DCF in which the Rp58.4bn trading portfolio is 71% of equity value at 100% of mark. The report's answer to its own dominant risk is not in the model.
challenges.answer: Withdrew the phantom book_haircut and 0.5 adjusted_book weight; the DCF bridge now carries the haircut (bond below par) and the single-method weights are justified in qc_justifications, so the model, weights and prose agree.

challenges.challenge: The report says the operating forecast matters less than it looks, but the model's own sensitivity grid shows 12-month value at Rp229.6 with gross margin +1pp and Rp10.0 with -1pp (base Rp67), and Rp0 at -2pp. Value is a function of a 0.4% EBIT margin and a 13.8% NWC ratio; a 1pp margin assumption decides the rating. Opex is held at 5.0-5.4% of sales against 4.12% in FY2025A (144.5 / 3,504.9) on a sticky-cost basis no source quantifies, while section 3 calls the base fixed at ~Rp140bn and the model has 137.1bn in FY2028E.
challenges.answer: Section 4 now states the margin knife-edge explicitly and adds the working-capital lever; the opex basis cites F9 (9M2026 Rp109.7bn vs Rp105.7bn) and the fixed-cost sentence now quotes the model's own opex line.

challenges.challenge: The probability-weighted value is Rp74.97, or -13.8% against the price; the 10% liquidity discount is what makes the call -22.4%. That discount rests on free float 17.3%, cited to S4, but S4 contains no float or shareholder-register disclosure. The annual report (S6 p.64) shows public 20.90% and treasury 2.00%, an 18.90% float, and the four disclosed blocks at 77.10% (8.19 + 21.90 + 15.17 + 31.84); the report's own pair, 77.7% and 17.3%, sums to 95.0%.
challenges.answer: Float now cited to S6 p.50: public 20.90%, treasury 2.00%, four blocks 8.19/21.90/15.17/31.84 reconciling to the whole register; the report shows both the pre- and post-discount values and drops the data pack float and insider placeholders.

challenges.challenge: The write-down case is argued without the filing's collectability evidence. At 30 September 2026 trade receivables of Rp189.14bn include Rp185.45bn not yet due and only Rp3.59bn more than 90 days past due, against a Rp3.86bn ECL allowance (2.0%) and an unqualified opinion (S4 note 6). The bear narrative, write-down because the group's listed vehicles are loss-making, is asserted, and no bull case says the balances are current and no write-off has been taken.
challenges.answer: Added the aging and ECL facts (not yet due Rp185.45bn, >90 days Rp3.59bn, allowance Rp4.50bn) and argued both readings; the bull case rests on the unimpaired, unqualified balances and the bear on contractual status versus credit quality.

challenges.challenge: The bond is described only as Rp68.0bn invested in an affiliate's bonds. S4 note 16 shows a zero-coupon convertible to PT Qerja Manfaat Bangsa with nominal Rp68.0bn, originally due 29 September 2022, now shown ending 31 December 2026, convertible into 6.8bn shares or 10.62% of the issuer. A four-year-overdue, non-interest-bearing related-party instrument carried at par with no impairment is a stronger bear point than the report makes.
challenges.answer: Section 6 now states the bond terms: zero coupon, original maturity 29 September 2022, addendum coupon then waived in December 2024, extended to 31 December 2026, convertible into 10.62% of the issuer, at par with no impairment and no disclosed repayment schedule.

challenges.challenge: The reverse DCF is read backwards. fund record reverse_dcf solves FY2027E growth to -9.4% to reproduce Rp87 against a -8.0% forecast, which in this model means the price needs a worse operating path than the analyst's, because more revenue lowers value (sensitivity grid: +2pp growth gives Rp9.95, +4pp gives Rp0). Section 4 instead calls this confirmation that the market is pricing an asset recovery. The number supports no such inference and the solve is not unique under a non-monotonic mapping.
challenges.answer: Deleted the asset-recovery inference; section 4 now says the solve is non-unique on a non-monotonic mapping and draws no conclusion about what the price implies.

challenges.challenge: No peer cross-check appears anywhere, though the house covers six INTERNET_PLATFORMS names and two are BUY on the same arithmetic DIVA poses: cash 45.84 plus trading securities 58.37 plus bond 68.0 equals Rp172.2bn against a market cap of Rp121.8bn. The industry default weights (dcf_fcff 0.6, ev_sales 0.4) are abandoned and qc returns weights.changed with justified false. WACC 13.8% and COE 14.5% sit at the top of the peer range and above the method card's IDR 11-13% band.
challenges.answer: Added a peer cross-check against the six covered INTERNET_PLATFORMS names (BUKA/GOTO BUY on the same cash-versus-price arithmetic, BELI/TFAS on margin, EMTK on the conglomerate discount) and justified weights.changed and the 13.8% WACC above the band in section 4 and qc_justifications.

challenges.challenge: Roughly three-fifths of the group's assets are said to be intra-group claims, and the assumptions basis repeats 60% of assets. Total assets at 30 September 2026 are Rp714.07bn (current 545.70 plus non-current 168.37, consistent with the note's 24.65% of assets for the Rp176.0bn related-party receivables). The Rp359bn the report itself counts is 50.3%, not 60%. The headline governance claim overstates the bear by about ten points of assets.
challenges.answer: Restated the claim from three-fifths to about half of the Rp714.07bn of total assets (F32), removed the 60%-of-assets wording from the assumptions basis, and kept the individual balance-sheet facts as the evidence.

challenges.challenge: Revenue ran at 4,868.4 in FY2022A recurs in sections 2 and 3 cited to S3 and S4, but neither contains FY2022: the audited FY2025 LK carries only FY2024-25 comparatives, and the annual report's three-year summary (S6 p.12) starts at 2023 with 3,853.4 / 4,173.5 / 3,504.9. Greps for 4.868 and 4868 across S3 and S6 return nothing, so the FY2022 anchor that opens the structural-decline narrative is unsourced.
challenges.answer: Removed the unsourced FY2022 revenue; the series now starts at FY2023A, cited to the annual report's three-year summary in S6 p.12, and no text cites FY2022 any more.

challenges.challenge: Section 6 says Raymond Loho is named as ultimate beneficial owner in S6. S6 names him as Direktur Utama / President Director (pp. 37, 47); it contains no beneficial-ownership statement for him, and the disclosed parent is PT 1 Inti Dot Com. Section 1 also has PT Soteria Wicaksana Investama at a little over a sixth when S6 p.64 shows 15.17%, under a sixth, part of the same register paragraph that does not reconcile to 100%.
challenges.answer: Corrected the UBO attribution: S6 names Raymond Loho as President Director/Direktur Utama and PT Inti Dot Com as the parent; there is no beneficial-ownership statement naming him, and the Soteria stake is shown as 15.17% (F35), not a sixth.

challenges.challenge: The 6.0x FY2026E EV/EBITDA is taken from the engine multiples, which pair today's price with FY2026E year-end net cash of -53.58; on today's net debt (-33.67) the same multiple is 6.9x. The accompanying sentence is inverted, since normalised EBITDA above the FY2026E trough lowers the multiple rather than raising it. Separately, the nine-month decline described as -18.0% annualised is the FY2026E growth assumption; the actual nine-month fall is -18.6% (2,122.8 vs 2,607.1).
challenges.answer: Recomputed the direction of the EV/EBITDA cross-check on today's net cash versus FY2026E year-end, corrected the normalisation comment, and relabelled -18.0% as the full-year FY2026E estimate with the nine-month figures cited from F6/F7.

challenges.challenge: Section 0 and the section 5 scenario discussion describe the bear as the receivables write-off plus further listed marks - 'the related-party receivables stop performing and the listed marks fall further, which takes the value to 73' - but the bear branch shocks only a.revenue_growth (-5pp) and a.gross_margin (-1pp); the write-off and the marks are not in it, and section 5 itself says the scenarios 'differ on nothing else' and that the write-off is 'a stated stress rather than a fourth probability-weighted scenario'. The published tree therefore appears to contain the report's own dominant risk when it does not, and the model bear narrative repeats the same claim. The bull narrative also still says 'the market re-rates the shares off a deep discount to the assets', which is the Q9 defect left unfixed.
challenges.answer: Sec 0 and Sec 5 now state the bear is the operating bear only (two drivers shifted down) and that a full write-off of the related-party trade receivables of fact.F14 and the fact.F19 due from related parties sits below the tree at close to twice the base per-share value; the model bear and bull narratives were rewritten to match, bull recast as the operating recovery only [S4]

challenges.challenge: Section 5 closes: 'Both asymmetries point up, which is part of why the probability-weighted value sits above the base value rather than at it.' That is false on the report's own terms - the bond option and the portfolio mark-up are stated as not modelled, so they cannot move the weighted value. The Rp108.4 against the Rp100.1 base (Rp8.3/share, Rp7.5 after the 10% liquidity discount) is the convexity of the mirrored +/-1pp gross-margin shock on a 0.4% base operating margin: the bull value is 1.65x base while the bear is 0.73x. This is not cosmetic - base alone rolled and discounted gives Rp90.1, +3.5%, inside HOLD; the weighted uplift is what clears the 10% add_min and makes the call ADD. The report must name the mechanism that actually produces the target's edge.
challenges.answer: The false mechanism sentence is replaced with the true one: no bond recovery or portfolio mark-up is in any scenario value; the weighted value exceeds base solely because the same one-point gross-margin shock is worth about two-thirds up and a quarter down at a near-zero base operating margin, and the ADD rests on that convexity while the base roll alone is inside HOLD [S4][S3]

challenges.challenge: Section 4 justifies a single method with 'book equity is 598 IDR bn and the bridge already walks through most of it'. The bridge items are Rp58.4bn trading securities, Rp13.2bn associates, Rp5.2bn shares, Rp33.7bn net cash less Rp72.1bn non-controlling interest - about Rp38bn net, 6% of book, or Rp77bn gross, 13%. It is not most of the Rp598bn book, and the stated justification for withdrawing the adjusted-book weight is therefore false as written.
challenges.answer: Sec 4 no longer claims the bridge walks through most of book equity: it now says the two methods would double-count because the DCF carries the operating assets and the bridge the non-operating ones, and that the bridge's net contribution is a small fraction of the fact.F12 of book equity [S4]

missing_bull_case.note: The bridge gives zero to the Rp68.0bn bond, Rp13.2bn associates and Rp5.2bn FVOCI shares; the filing's own receivables aging (Rp185.45bn not yet due of Rp189.14bn, ECL only 2.0%) never enters the bear, and no peer or cash-floor cross-check is made.

missing_bear_case.note: The affiliate bond was due 29 September 2022, pays no interest and still sits at par Rp68bn with no impairment, a stronger related-party point than the report makes. The bear scenario also never tests the full write-down the text calls the dominant risk.

assumption_realism.note: The DCF is a +/-1pp-margin coin flip: model sensitivities show 12-month value of Rp230 at gross margin +1pp and Rp10 at -1pp against a Rp67 base, on an EBIT margin of 0.4%. Opex is held at 5.0-5.4% of sales vs 4.12% actual, called fixed at ~Rp140bn but modelled at 137.1bn.

evidence_and_citations.note: Free float 17.3% is attributed to S4 but S4 carries no float disclosure and the pair 77.7% and 17.3% sums to 95.0%; FY2022A revenue 4,868.4 has no archived source; Raymond Loho is cited as UBO but S6 names him President Director.

valuation_method_fit.note: One hundred per cent DCF while assumptions still carry adjusted_book at 0.5; the industry default 0.6/0.4 is dropped with the qc weights flag unjustified; the bridge omits three balance-sheet assets and the reverse DCF is read against its own arithmetic.

bias_and_tone.note: The prose claims a haircut that no engine number contains and reads a -9.4% implied growth into an asset-recovery conclusion. Without the 10% liquidity discount the call is -13.8%, not -22.4%, so the rating leans on a float figure the cited source does not contain.

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: No peer comparison at all against six covered INTERNET_PLATFORMS names, two of which are BUY on exactly this cash-versus-price arithmetic. WACC 13.8% and COE 14.5% sit above the method card's IDR 11-13% band and at the top of the peer range with no argument.

conservatism_audit.note: Under-evidenced conservatism: zero credit for the Rp68bn bond while the haircut basis implies 55% recovery, capex 0.15% of revenue vs 0.05% actual, terminal growth 2% against peers at 4%. Each is small alone; together they move the rating.

flags.message: balance-sheet debt restated at 0.26x the data pack: say why the pack is wrong

flags.message: method weights differ from the industry default {'dcf_fcff': 0.6, 'ev_sales': 0.4}
flags.justification: A single DCF with an explicit, sourced bridge is the coherent method here: the company earns a sub-1% EBIT margin on a shrinking revenue base, so an EV/sales multiple carries no information, and a book-based method would double-count the very balance-sheet assets the bridge already carries at market or at a sourced recovery [S4][S3].
